newsitem.title: BULGARIA: HIGH LEV, DEFICIT MAY PUT AT RISK BULGARIAN RECOVERY.
newsitem.headline: HIGH LEV, DEFICIT MAY PUT AT RISK BULGARIAN RECOVERY.

text.p: Bulgaria's currency board system, due to be launched next month to stabilise the crumbling economy, faces serious challenges from a high budget deficit and an overvalued fixed lev/mark rate, economists warn despite government's optimism.

Bulgaria's government reached an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday on this year's draft budget deficit of 6.2 percent, higher than IMF-recommended 3.8 percent and announced a fixed lev/mark rate of 1,000.

"Success of the currency board will depend on how soon confidence in the banks is restored, privatisation and fiscal discipline," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Emerging Market Analyst Stuart Parkinson told Reuters.

"I think that financing the budget deficit is potentially a challange for the government given they do not want to increase significantly the domestic debt burden," said Salomon Brothers Emergin Markets Research Vice President David Boren.
Other analysts warned the high budget deficit could fuel inflation and raise interest rates, but local economists echoed the government's insistance for a higher, but sustainable budget deficit.

"Given the expectations of continuing economic decline in the short-term, the low budget deficit was unrealistic. You can not collect high revenues in a shrinking economy," said Bulgarian Investment Bank economist Galina Dimitrova.

Up to 3.4 percent of the deficit is expected to be funded from privatisation proceeds, said Finance Minister Muravei Radev, but the new reformist government needs to leap into sell-offs to compensate previous governments' reluctance to sell.
"We want to see privatisation making more progress in selling state owned companies, particularly, the crown jewels," said Parkinson.
Bulgaria has fallen behind pledges to the World Bank to privatise 25 percent of state assets under an agreement signed last year. Only 18.5 percent of assets have been sold off so far.
A World Bank mission is due to arrive in Sofia in the second half of June to evaluate Bulgaria's performance under an agreement which has earmarked some $280 million for Bulgaria.
Further tranches from a $510 million IMF standby agreement are also hinged on Bulgaria meeting World Bank restructuring targets.

"The lev/mark peg rate is a too strong level," said ING Bank emerging markets economist Parvoleta Shtereva, echoing other economists apprehensions that an overvalued lev would hinder production and exports and stimulate imports, resulting in a high trade deficit and slower economic growth.
Bulgarian Academy of Sciences estimates showed that at the time of introduction the rate should be between 1,300 and 1,400 to the mark. But Boren saw the fixed rate as reasonable.

"We can expect up to three months of stability, unless privatisation speeds up over the summer. Financing the budget deficit is going to require interest rates to go up, which may undermine awaited stability," said an economist who declined to be named.

High yields now and expectations for low exchange rate risk under the currency board sytem attracted around $130 million investment in government paper from foreign investors in the past several months, said a finance ministry official.
"I expect interest rates to fluctuate around lower than current levels after the currency board is introduced," head of Finance Ministry's Treasury and Debt Department Plamen Oresharski told Reuters.
The average yield to maturity on four-week government paper auctioned since Friday ranged between 3.81-3.69 percent.

The draft budget needs yet to be passed by the cabinet and parliament by the end of the month, before the currency board system is launched on July 1, with the aim to restore confidence in the volatile currency and troubled banks.
Under the system all levs in circulation must be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves of around $1 billion and the 1,000 lev/mark peg comes in effect from July 1.
Despite future pitfalls, Radev remained optimistic. "We have all reasons to successfully introduce and sustain the currency board arrangement," he told reporters. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
